The Tasmanian pygmy possum, Cercartetus lepidus, is one of the smallest diprotodont marsupials, and its diminutive size imposes striking physiological constraints. Respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions reveal a maximum basal metabolic rate of 18.77 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 18.77 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a value that reflects the high mass-specific costs of endothermy in a mammal of such minimal mass. This metabolic intensity is consistent with the elevated rates observed in other small dasyurid and burramyid species, where heat conservation is perpetually challenged by a large surface-area-to-volume ratio. Adult females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 10 grams [Wwi = 10 grams], though field data indicate a typical range of 7 to 10 grams (7-10 grams) [Wwi = 7-10 grams], placing Cercartetus lepidus among the lightest of all marsupials. This minimal somatic investment is coupled with a remarkably brief gestation period of 12.5 days [tg = 12.5 days] at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], an exceptionally short intrauterine duration that is characteristic of the family Burramyidae and necessitates a highly altricial neonatal state at parturition.

The reproductive strategy of Cercartetus lepidus is heavily influenced by its tiny body size and the energetic demands of lactation. Females typically produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], with each litter containing four pups [N_R_i = each litter containing four pups], a modest litter size that balances maternal investment against the high metabolic overhead of milk production. The combination of one litter each year with four pups per litter yields a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.011 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.011 pups per day], but this is more naturally expressed in the annual context of the species' seasonal breeding. Reproductive output is therefore concentrated into a single annual event, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a body mass of around 10 grams [Wwi = around 10 grams] for adult females. The neonates themselves emerge from the birth canal at an extraordinarily small wet weight of just 0.1 grams [Wwb = 0.1 grams] at birth, a value that underscores the extreme altriciality of marsupial newborns and the reliance on a protracted period of pouch life and lactation for further development. This birth mass is among the lowest recorded for any mammal, highlighting the evolutionary trade-off between rapid gestation and the need to transfer the burden of growth to the post-parturition, milk-dependent phase.

Post-natal development in the Tasmanian pygmy possum proceeds through a series of tightly scheduled milestones while the young remain dependent on the mother. Weaning, defined as the cessation of milk dependence and the transition to a diet of pollen, nectar, and small invertebrates, occurs approximately 50 days after birth [tx = approximately 50 days after birth] under the standard thermoneutral conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This weaning age is relatively brief for a small marsupial, likely facilitated by the rapid growth enabled by both milk of high nutritional quality and the early onset of exogenous feeding on carbohydrate-rich floral resources. Following weaning, juveniles enter a period of rapid somatic growth and behavioral maturation. The attainment of sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to breed, is reached at approximately 91.5 days from birth [tp = approximately 91.5 days from birth], which corresponds to roughly 3 months of age, based on the measurements recorded at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This early pubertal onset is typical of small, short-lived mammals that prioritize early reproduction to offset high extrinsic mortality rates.

Longevity in Cercartetus lepidus is constrained by its high metabolic pace and small body size, leading to a relatively short life expectancy compared to larger mammals. The maximum recorded lifespan in wild populations has been documented at 4 years [am = 4 years], based on longitudinal trapping studies, with this value determined for individuals measured at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This lifespan, while brief in absolute terms, is nevertheless considerable for a mammal weighing only 10 grams, and the value of 4 years [am = 4 years] is consistent with predictions from allometric scaling relationships for small insectivorous-nectarivorous marsupials at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This life-history profile, characterized by rapid development, high initial metabolic investment, and relatively brief total longevity, aligns closely with predictions from allometric scaling relationships for small insectivorous-nectarivorous marsupials.

Comparative ecological and physiological studies further contextualize the life history of the Tasmanian pygmy possum within the broader burramyid radiation. The exceptionally short gestation period of 12.5 days [tg = 12.5 days] observed at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C] is a shared trait with its congener, the eastern pygmy possum (Cercartetus nanus), though Cercartetus lepidus achieves an even smaller neonatal mass of 0.1 grams [Wwb = 0.1 grams], reflecting its more extreme miniaturization. The maximum recorded longevity of 4 years [am = 4 years] for this species is similar to that reported for the western pygmy possum (Cercartetus concinnus), suggesting a conserved lifespan within the genus when temperature conditions are comparable at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. The dietary switch at weaning, occurring at 50 days after birth [tx = 50 days after birth], coincides with the seasonal peak in floral resource abundance in its Tasmanian habitat, indicating a tight phenological coupling between reproductive timing and food availability at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Adult females, weighing up to 10 grams, and with a maximum recorded body mass of 10 grams [Wwi = 10 grams], exhibit a remarkable ability to accumulate fat reserves in the tail, which serves as an energy store for periods of resource scarcity or during the energetically demanding lactation phase.
